source: MAFF General Directorate of Agriculture, បច្ចេកទេសដាំដុះដំណាំចេក (Techniques for Banana Cultivation), 2019, section I.3 (លក្ខណៈរូបសាស្ត្រដំណាំចេក)
text:
Roots (អួស): Banana has a shallow, wide-spreading fibrous root system rather than a deep taproot. Roots are white when young and darken to brown or black with age. A healthy clump can produce several hundred roots (the source cites up to around 400 roots per stool in good soil), with most of the active feeder roots concentrated in the top 20-60cm of soil and spreading out laterally roughly 1-1.5m from the base. Because the root system is shallow, banana is highly sensitive to both waterlogging and drought, and its roots are also easily damaged by careless hoeing or weeding close to the base.

Pseudostem/trunk (ដើម): What looks like a banana tree's trunk is not true wood but a pseudostem formed from tightly overlapping leaf sheaths wrapped around each other. It typically reaches 2.4-3.4m in height. The true stem is the underground corm (ដើមពិត), a swollen, disc-shaped structure roughly 30cm across that holds the growing points (buds) from which suckers and, eventually, the flower stalk emerge.

Leaves (ស្លិក): Banana leaves are large, elongated, and fast-growing, typically 70-100cm wide and 140-240cm long depending on variety and growing conditions. New leaves continually replace old ones, with older leaves yellowing and drying as new growth emerges from the crown.

Inflorescence bud and flower (ត្រយ៉ង/ផ្កា): The flower bud, often called the "banana heart," emerges from the growth point roughly 7-9 months after planting, with the whole flower stalk taking about a month to fully emerge. The inflorescence is covered by dark purple-red bracts that peel back to reveal rows of flowers; female flowers (which develop into fruit) are in the first layers, with male flowers in the layers that follow toward the tip.

Fruit and bunch (ផ្លែ/ត្រាប់): A full bunch typically carries multiple hands (ស៉ង), commonly around 6 but sometimes up to 11 depending on variety, with each hand holding 8-20 individual fingers. Fruit takes roughly 60-90 days to mature after flowering, depending on variety and climate, and matures from green to yellow (or in some cases red) as it ripens. Some varieties are naturally seedless (parthenocarpic) and are propagated only vegetatively, while seeded types produce small black seeds embedded in the flesh.
